n0001.title: Spider Silk
n0001.gist: Spider silk's layered structure gives it unmatched strength and toughness, driving its natural uses and artificial synthesis.
n0001.question: Spider silk — why is it both strong and tough enough to inspire artificial replication?

n0002.title: What Spiders Use Silk For
n0002.gist: Spiders spin silk from specialized glands for many purposes—trapping prey, building nests, ballooning, and signaling—with silk also central to courtship and mating.
n0002.question: Spider silk — what roles does it play in a spider's life and mating?

n0008.title: Functions of spider silk
n0008.gist: Spiders use silk as sticky traps, restraints for prey, sensory lines, nests, and lines for suspension or flight, varying its thickness by purpose, and occasionally eat it as food.

n0011.title: Silk and courtship
n0011.gist: All spiders produce silk even without building webs; female silk carries male vibratory courtship signals, while webs and draglines spread female sex pheromones, though male silk's mating role is little studied.

n0013.title: Properties
n0013.gist: Spider silk's hierarchical molecular structure and composition give it unusual combined strength, elasticity, and toughness, rivaling steel and Kevlar, plus strong adhesive properties.
n0013.question: Properties — why does spider silk combine strength, stretch, and stickiness so well? (several measures)

n0014.title: Structural
n0014.gist: Spider silk's strength comes from hard crystalline beta-sheet regions interlocking with a stretchy amorphous matrix, further tuned by compounds that keep it moist, acidic, and resistant to microbes.

n0022.title: Mechanical
n0022.gist: Dragline spider silk combines strength and stretch to absorb more energy before breaking than steel or Kevlar, with stiffness, toughness, density, and behavior under heat or water varying by species.

n0049.title: Adhesive
n0049.gist: Spider silk's adhesive attachment discs form from a two-part pyriform secretion that hardens instantly into a durable, biodegradable glue-like bond whose stickiness is controlled by the spinnerets.

n0052.title: Uses
n0052.gist: Every spider makes several kinds of silk, each suited to different uses such as trapping prey, reproducing, dispersing, feeding, nesting, and signaling, reflecting millions of years of evolving complexity.
n0052.question: Uses — what jobs does spider silk perform across a spider's life? (several examples)

n0056.title: Silk types
n0056.gist: Different glands produce distinct silk types—dragline, capture-spiral, egg-sac, wrapping, sticky, and attachment silks—each with properties matched to its specific structural or functional role.
n0056.question: Silk types — how do different glands supply silk suited to each specific task? (a classification)

n0057.title: Overview of silk types
n0057.gist: Spiders produce several distinct silk types—major and minor ampullate, flagelliform, piriform, tubuliform, aciniform, and aggregate—each made in a specific gland and suited to a specific structural or adhesive role.

n0064.title: Properties by silk type
n0064.gist: Different glands yield silks with distinct roles: dragline silk for web frames, flagelliform for sticky capture lines, tubuliform for stiff egg sacs, and aciniform for tough prey-wrapping, among other specialized uses.

n0068.title: Synthesis and fibre spinning
n0068.gist: Spiders pull silk on demand from glands by a pulling-based process called pultrusion, rather than growing it continuously, with gland anatomy controlling the fiber's final structure.
n0068.question: Synthesis and fibre spinning — how does a spider's gland turn liquid protein into solid fiber? (gland anatomy)

n0069.title: Spinning process
n0069.gist: Unlike other biomaterials, spider silk is pulled on demand from glands by a pulling-based process called pultrusion rather than squeezed out or continuously grown, with the fiber drawn through multiple gland types.

n0074.title: Silk gland anatomy
n0074.gist: The gland's tail, storage sac, funnel, and tapering duct progressively concentrate, align, and acidify the liquid protein until shear and pH changes condense it into a solid, organized fiber.

n0087.title: Araneus gland example
n0087.gist: A single garden cross spider contains hundreds of specialized glands—pyriform, ampullate, aciniform, tubuliform, aggregate, and coronate—each dedicated to a distinct silk function, from attachment points to egg-sac lining.

n0095.title: Artificial synthesis
n0095.gist: Replicating spider silk artificially requires both producing silk-like feedstock proteins and engineering spinning conditions that mimic a spider's gland, a challenge only partly solved so far.
n0095.question: Artificial synthesis — why has replicating natural spider silk proven so difficult? (several approaches)

n0096.title: Feedstock
n0096.gist: Producing silk-like feedstock means extracting, purifying, and spinning long, complex silk proteins from organisms such as bark spiders, silkworms, E. coli, goats, and plants, each yielding fibers with different strength and stretch.

n0103.title: Geometry
n0103.gist: Because spider silk proteins alone cannot form fibers, researchers use complex delivery methods—needles, superhydrophobic surfaces, microfluidics, and electrospinning—to approximate a spider's duct and force proteins into solid fiber form.

n0119.title: Synthetic spider silk
n0119.gist: Genetically engineered bacteria, yeast, plants, silkworms, and other animals can produce spider silk-like proteins, but wet-spun fibers remain thicker, weaker, and less flexible than natural dragline silk, despite growing commercial research efforts.

n0132.title: Research
n0132.gist: A chronological table of significant publications traces how scientists progressively uncovered spider silk's chemistry, gene sequence, structure, mechanics, and spinning process, and pursued synthetic replication.
n0132.question: Research — which studies built current understanding of spider silk's structure and synthesis? (a chronological table)

n0135.title: Human uses
n0135.gist: Humans have long tried to harvest and weave spider silk into fabric and tools, and though mass production remains difficult, spider silk finds niche medical, scientific, and technological applications.
n0135.question: Human uses — what practical uses have people found for spider silk despite production difficulties? (several examples)

n0136.title: Early production history
n0136.gist: From 1709 onward, inventors wove silk from spider cocoons or harvested threads, but none achieved commercial-scale production, leaving spider silk limited to rare items like a hand-woven golden cape and violin strings.

n0141.title: Medicine
n0141.gist: Traditional Carpathian healers covered wounds with spider silk tube linings, likely benefiting from its antiseptic and vitamin K clotting properties, while modern research has explored its use in nerve regeneration.

n0144.title: Science and technology
n0144.gist: Spider silk has served as crosshairs in optical instruments, enabled fine diffraction patterns for optical communication, formed high-resolution biolenses, and suspended fusion targets thanks to its elasticity and light atomic composition.
